description: We’re a group of cybersecurity professionals and software developers working on a tool to solve the challenge “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” The tool allows users to pick variables and visualize how they change over time. This will tell them what, where, how much and if changes are statistically significant. We have taken a cybersecurity approach to ensuring data integrity and validation throughout the pipeline.
summary:
MegavirTrace is a free web tool that gives anyone an honest, checkable answer to the question "Is this place really changing?" Pick any place on Earth (a city, a country, one of 138 preset regions or a box you draw) and one of 31 variables from 23 NASA datasets: temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, vegetation, sea level, sea ice, NO₂, aerosols and more. It answers the challenge's four questions: what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is significant.

A single deterministic engine computes every number, and its data are cross-checked against NASA Giovanni. Two independent trend tests must agree, corrected for year-to-year memory, and a non-significant result says how many more years of data would be needed. A cell map shows where the change is happening, Compare tests whether two regions really differ, and 20 detective cases investigate real events such as Europe's 2003 heatwave. An optional AI scientist explains results but never computes; every number it writes is checked.

Climate headlines are easy to overstate or dismiss. MegavirTrace lets students, journalists and citizens check change in their own place with real NASA data and honest statistics.
details:
What it does and how it works

MegavirTrace answers one question for any place on Earth: is it really changing? You pick a variable and a place (one of about 39,000 cities, states and countries, 138 preset regions, or a box you draw). The app then answers the challenge's four questions: what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is significant.

It covers 31 variables from 23 NASA datasets, including GISTEMP, MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, GPCP, GLDAS, MODIS, AIRS, OMI, GRACE/GRACE-FO, NASA-SSH, SMAP, CERES, NSIDC sea ice, OCO-2 and MiCASA. Data are fetched with NASA Earthdata Login, CMR and OPeNDAP, requesting only the fields needed (for MERRA-2 aerosols, 0.35 GB instead of 36 GB). Each product is converted to everyday units, put on a common grid, checked, and stored as a versioned dataset.

One deterministic engine computes every number. A trend counts as significant only when the Mann–Kendall test and least squares both agree, after correcting for year-to-year memory (autocorrelation). The rate is Sen's slope with a 95% range, and robustness checks test both halves of the record and leave out each year in turn. A result that isn't significant says how many more years of data would be needed. A cell map shows where inside the region the change happens, with false-discovery control. Compare tests whether two regions really differ, and "Related variables" tests whether two variables move together.

Twenty detective cases turn real events (Europe's 2003 heatwave, Pakistan's 2022 floods, Australia's Black Summer, the 2020 lockdowns) into guided investigations computed live from the data. NASA GLOBE school measurements and NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate projections appear beside the trend as context.

An optional AI scientist (Claude or Z.ai GLM) turns questions into engine runs and explains the results. It never computes: every number it writes is checked against the stored results, and if any check fails, the plain verdict is shown instead.

Benefits and intended impact

Climate claims are easy to overstate or dismiss. MegavirTrace lets students, teachers, journalists, local decision-makers and curious citizens check change in their own place, with real NASA data and statistics they can verify. Every result cites its dataset and DOI, can be downloaded as CSV, Excel or PDF, and comes with a Jupyter notebook that recomputes every number. An open, read-only API and embeddable cards let others reuse the results. The site works in English and Spanish, on phones, and offline after one visit, so it can reach classrooms and communities with weak connections.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

-Backend: Python (NumPy, SciPy, xarray, h5py, netCDF4, earthaccess), FastAPI, and PostgreSQL with PostGIS in Docker.

-Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js and React, with MapLibre GL maps drawn from OpenStreetMap data (OpenFreeMap). Natural Earth and GeoNames supply the places.

-Testing: pytest, plus Playwright browser tests with axe-core accessibility checks.

-AI: the Anthropic SDK (Claude) and Z.ai.

-Hardware and hosting: a single Linux server runs everything, behind nginx with Let's Encrypt; the code is on GitHub. No special hardware was needed.

-AI-assisted development: we used AI coding assistants (Claude Code), and every method is documented and tested.

What makes it creative

Honesty is the feature. The app says "not significant yet, needs about N more years" rather than overclaiming. Detective cases make trend analysis feel like solving a mystery, but the story only says where to look, and the data supply the findings. The AI is used for what it does well, explaining, and never for computing. Satellite trends sit beside measurements by GLOBE schools and volunteers.

Factors we considered

-Statistical honesty: false alarms were measured in simulation (at most 4.7%).

-Data accuracy: our series were checked against NASA's official GISTEMP series (r = 0.9997) and against NASA Giovanni for air temperature (r = 0.9998) and rainfall (r = 0.995).

-Transparency: DOIs, data versions and reproducible notebooks.

-Clear limits: a trend is not a cause, reanalysis is not a direct measurement, and projections are context, not forecasts.

-Accessibility and inclusion: two languages, phone-first design, dark mode and automated accessibility tests.

-Safety and cost: no sign-in or cookies, strict request checks, rate limits, and daily AI caps.
